segments.text: These are a thousand pendulums. They all started in almost exactly the same place, within a hundred-thousandth of a degree. Watch what happens.

A few seconds later, they have nothing in common. This is chaos. And it's the reason your weather app can't tell you if it'll rain two weeks from now. So I wanted to see it for myself. I programmed it from scratch, and it turned out stranger, and more beautiful, than I expected.

Let's start simple. One pendulum: a weight on a rod. Physics has understood this for four hundred years. Give it a push, and it swings back and forth, on the same path, forever. If I know where it is now, I can tell you exactly where it'll be in a thousand years. Predictable. Boring.
Now, hang a second pendulum off the end of the first. That's it. One more rod.

And the motion goes completely wild. The tip loops, flips, hesitates, and never follows the same path twice. Same physics. Same gravity. No randomness anywhere in the code. So where does this come from?

To simulate it, you need these two equations. They look scary, but all they say is: given where the arms are, and how fast they're moving, here's how they'll speed up or slow down. The computer steps forward a tiny bit of time, and repeats. Again and again.

My first version did those steps the simplest way, called Euler's method. And it was wrong. Watch the pendulum on the left. It's gaining energy out of nowhere, swinging higher and higher, until it's spinning like a propeller. That's impossible. Every tiny step added a tiny error, and the errors piled up.

So I switched to a smarter method, called Runge-Kutta, which checks the slope four times per step. Now the energy stays constant to one part in a million, even after two minutes. Now we can trust what we see.
Here's the experiment. Two pendulums, one degree apart. For a moment, you can barely tell them apart. Then they start to drift. And then, they're doing completely different things.
Okay, one degree is a lot. What if I make the difference smaller? A thousand times smaller? A million times smaller?

So I did this. A thousand pendulums, each a tiny fraction of a degree from its neighbor. The whole group starts within a hundred-thousandth of a degree. The tips are less than the width of a virus apart.
For ten seconds, they move as one. Then the rainbow appears. The colors are those tiny differences, finally becoming visible. And then, it's chaos.

Here's what's going on. This is the gap between two pendulums over time. Each line on this graph is a thousand times bigger than the one below it. And the gap climbs them like stairs, at a steady rate. That's exponential growth. Every tiny difference gets multiplied, again and again, until it's as big as the whole motion.
So what if we start a thousand times closer? It doesn't buy us a thousand times more time. It buys us about seven seconds. That's chaos. Not randomness, but extreme sensitivity to where you start.
And honestly? It's also just beautiful.
You can play with this yourself. The link is in the description. Drag the pendulums, change how close they start, and make your own.

And this isn't just about pendulums. In 1961, a meteorologist named Edward Lorenz rounded one number in a weather simulation, and accidentally discovered that weather works exactly like this. What he saw next had a shape. That's the next video.
